scenes.headline: Women start the race. They rarely finish it.
scenes.subtext: Women hold 33% of entry-level corporate jobs in India. By the C-suite? 17%. The leakage happens silently, at every rung of the ladder.

stat.label: of C-suite positions in India's private sector are held by women — McKinsey Women in Workplace 2025

scenes.title: Three invisible forces — glass ceiling, broken rung, glass cliff
scenes.body: The glass ceiling is the invisible barrier that stops women from reaching the top, even when they're qualified. But newer research has found two more forces: the 'broken rung' — where women are blocked at the very first promotion to manager — and the 'glass cliff' — where women are given leadership only in crisis situations, set up to fail.
scenes.analogy: Imagine a building with a transparent floor at level 7. Women can see the top — but they hit the floor before reaching it. And the ladder? The first rung is broken. And when someone does get pulled up, it's usually when the building is on fire.

left.label: Entry level
left.value: Women: 33% of roles (48% of university graduates)

right.label: C-suite
right.value: Women: 17% of roles — the drop happens at every rung

scenes.title: The three barriers decoded
scenes.intro: Glass ceiling, broken rung, glass cliff — and the pay gap that runs through all of them.

items.title: The Glass Ceiling — you can see the top but can't reach it
items.detail: In India's tech sector (IIT Kharagpur study, 2025): women are nearly half of junior roles but only 13% of top-level positions. At CEO/VP level, only 2 out of 28 CEO roles are held by women.
items.stat: 30.51% gender pay gap in India's tech sector — IIT Kharagpur 2025

items.title: The Broken Rung — blocked at the very first step
items.detail: McKinsey's 2025 report found India's biggest barrier isn't the CEO level — it's the first promotion from individual contributor to manager. Miss that rung and the entire ladder shifts.
items.stat: Women enter the formal workforce 7 years later than men on average (age 39 vs 32)

items.title: The Glass Cliff — leadership only when things are on fire
items.detail: Women are disproportionately appointed to leadership roles during crises. If they succeed, credit often goes elsewhere. If they fail, the narrative becomes 'women can't lead.' This is the glass cliff — a poisoned invitation to the top.
items.stat: Women executives showed greater performance consistency during COVID-19 — but received less credit

items.title: The Maternal Wall — invisible penalty for becoming a mother
items.detail: After having children, women are seen as less committed, less ambitious, less available. They get passed over for promotions and high-profile projects. The maternal wall is the most socially accepted form of workplace discrimination.
items.stat: India's new Labour Codes allow WFH after maternity leave — government acknowledgment of the maternal wall

items.title: The pay gap that widens as you rise
items.detail: The IIT Kharagpur 2025 study found the gender pay gap actually widens at higher income levels. Senior women earn proportionally less compared to senior men than junior women do compared to junior men. Success doesn't fix the gap. It deepens it.

scenes.title: Is India making progress?

left_items.label: Legal framework exists
left_items.detail: Equal Remuneration Act 1976, POSH Act 2013, maternity benefit protections — legal tools are in place

left_items.label: IT sector leading change
left_items.detail: IT and healthcare are India's most gender-inclusive sectors — remote work helped women retain careers

left_items.label: Corporate accountability growing
left_items.detail: SEBI mandates at least one woman director on listed company boards — compliance is near-universal now

right_items.label: 15% of boards track gender diversity
right_items.detail: McKinsey 2025: only 15% of corporate boards monitor gender diversity outcomes

right_items.label: Financial sector worst offender
right_items.detail: Women: 31% of entry-level in financial services, just 13% of C-suite

right_items.label: No mandatory pay transparency
right_items.detail: Unlike EU, India has no law requiring companies to disclose gender pay gaps

scenes.officer_framing: India has the legal framework — what's missing is enforcement, accountability, and a cultural shift in how ambition is perceived in women. The ceiling isn't glass anymore; it's become a one-way mirror.

scenes.title: India vs the world
scenes.body: India ranked 131st in WEF's Global Gender Gap Report 2025 — slipping 2 places from 129th. India is in the bottom 5 globally on 'Economic Participation and Opportunity'. For context: Bangladesh is ranked higher than India on gender economic parity.

scenes.title: Use this in SSB
scenes.pi_question: What is the glass ceiling and how does it affect women in India?
scenes.gd_line: The glass ceiling, broken rung, and glass cliff together explain why women start strong but rarely finish at the top. The solution isn't just legal — it requires changing how organisations measure success, track promotions, and define leadership potential.
lecturette_structure: Open: Women hold 33% of entry-level roles. Only 17% reach the C-suite. What happens in between?
Define the three barriers: glass ceiling, broken rung, glass cliff — one sentence each
Data: 30.51% pay gap in tech, 131st rank globally, maternal wall effect
What's working: SEBI mandate, POSH Act, IT sector progress
Close: Legal tools exist — enforcement and cultural change are the remaining gaps
scenes.pi_answer: Sir, the glass ceiling refers to the invisible barrier preventing women from reaching top leadership despite being qualified. In India, women hold 33% of entry-level roles but only 17% of C-suite positions. The problem starts even earlier at the 'broken rung' — the first promotion to manager. India has strong legal frameworks — Equal Remuneration Act, POSH Act, SEBI's board diversity mandate — but lacks mandatory pay transparency and robust enforcement. The path forward is accountability, not just aspiration.
scenes.one_liner: The ceiling isn't glass anymore — it's a one-way mirror. Women can't see it, but the gatekeepers above can.

questions.q: What is the 'broken rung' as opposed to the 'glass ceiling'?
options: Both mean the same thing — barriers to women's advancement
The broken rung is the specific barrier at the first promotion to manager — before women even reach the glass ceiling. Fix the rung, and the ceiling becomes reachable.
The broken rung refers to pay gaps at the senior level
questions.explanation: The glass ceiling is a mid-to-senior level barrier. The broken rung is earlier — and often more damaging because it stops the climb before it begins.

questions.q: A company claims it is gender-equal because 48% of its employees are women. As an officer, how would you evaluate this claim?
options: Accept it — 48% is near parity so the company is doing well
Probe further — what percentage of managers and senior leaders are women? Entry-level diversity means little if the promotion pipeline leaks at every rung.
Reject it — companies always lie about diversity
questions.explanation: Representation at entry level is the floor, not the ceiling. An officer's analysis looks at pipeline data, not just snapshot numbers.
